planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this dwarf Taiwanese woodland native resents winter wet more than the taller Disporopsis species, so avoid heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade, siting it where little else will grow densely under trees. This diminutive relative of Solomon's seal forms low, slowly spreading clumps of wiry, arching stems clad in thick, glossy, rounded, evergreen leaves that stay attractive through the coldest months in its hardiness range. Small, drooping, bell-shaped, creamy white flowers dangle from the leaf axils in early summer, mostly hidden beneath the foliage and more often discovered than displayed. Because it stays under a foot tall and spreads gradually by rhizome rather than running aggressively, it is best used as a refined edging or underplanting for larger ferns and hostas rather than as a fast groundcover for open ground.

common_name: Little Tickler Dwarf Northern Sea Oats

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, moist soil in dappled shade to partial sun; Little Tickler stays tight and upright without the flopping habit of the full-sized species, so it does not need the support that taller sea oats sometimes do.

directions: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in average garden soil in dappled shade to part sun, where this compact selection of the eastern native sea oats forms a dense, upright, non-flopping clump of narrow, bamboo-like leaves. In late summer it sends up the same flattened, dangling, oat-like seed heads typical of the species, though scaled down to suit the smaller plant, aging from green to a soft tan through autumn and persisting for winter interest. Its tidy habit and reduced self-sowing compared with the full-sized species make it a better fit for small woodland edges, rock gardens, and mixed perennial borders where the straight species would seed around too freely. Cut the previous season's foliage back in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to part shade; Goldbug (also sold as 'Chigger') is a slow-spreading dwarf form, so give it an uncrowded spot where its small size won't be swallowed by larger shade perennials.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to part shade, treating it as a miniature companion for mini hostas and other small-scale woodland plants. Goldbug is a dwarf, slow-spreading selection of Japanese fairy bells whose short, arching stems carry leaves that are more than half suffused with bright cream and yellow, streaked and banded with dark green, giving the clump an almost hosta-like look at only a few inches tall. Small, white, nodding bell flowers appear in spring and look disproportionately large against the diminutive foliage. Keep soil evenly moist and top-dress with leaf mold or compost; because it spreads gradually rather than running, it is best suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, or the front edge of a shaded border rather than broad-scale groundcover use.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in average to rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to full shade; this gold-leaved selection, originally found on Shikoku Island, Japan, holds its bright coloring best out of hot midday sun.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade, where the slow-spreading rhizomes gradually knit into a small, slowly expanding colony. Awa-no-tsuki is prized above other fairy bells selections for broad leaves that are mostly bright yellow with only a thin edging and tip of green, lighting up a shaded border far more boldly than green-leaved Disporum species. Small, nodding, white bell flowers appear beneath the foliage in spring, typical of the genus but secondary to the striking leaf color. It pairs well with blue- or dark-leaved hostas and ferns, and keeping soil consistently moist through summer helps prevent the thin-textured gold leaves from scorching.
